statement: A repeatable risk assessment method is defined, with acceptance criteria and criteria for performing assessments. The method identifies risks to confidentiality, integrity and availability within scope, assigns risk owners, and ranks risks by likelihood and impact. It is kept as a documented procedure and reviewed on a defined cycle.
why_asked: Without a set method, assessments give inconsistent results that cannot be compared or trusted for decisions.
how_to_ask: Ask for the method document and check it sets scales, acceptance criteria and triggers. Ask how consistency between assessors is ensured. Example probe: "If two teams assessed the same system, would they reach the same rating, and how do you know?"
question: Does your organization have a documented, repeatable method for assessing security risk?
expected_evidence: Risk assessment methodology or procedure; likelihood and impact scales; risk acceptance criteria; approval record; review history for the last two cycles
good_looks_like: The method defines scales, acceptance criteria, triggers for assessment and how owners are assigned. It requires covering confidentiality, integrity and availability, and shows how consistent results are checked. It is approved and reviewed.
test: Obtain the method. Check it defines criteria, triggers, scales and owner assignment. Apply it to two sample risks from the register and compare ratings. Pass if the method is approved and complete and the sample ratings follow it.
baseline_risk: Risk ratings are inconsistent and arbitrary, so treatment effort goes to the wrong places.

statement: A treatment is chosen for each assessed risk, the controls needed are determined, and a risk treatment plan is formulated. The treatment plan is approved, and residual risk accepted, in writing by those accountable for each risk. The plan is kept as a record and updated after each assessment cycle.
why_asked: Risks without a chosen treatment or recorded acceptance stay open, and no one is accountable for what remains.
how_to_ask: Ask for the treatment plan and pick risks from the register. Check each has a treatment, a control, an approval and recorded acceptance of what remains. Example probe: "Who signed off the residual risk on your top risk, and where is that recorded?"
question: Does your organization have a risk treatment plan approved, with residual risk accepted in writing by those accountable for each risk?
expected_evidence: Risk treatment plan; risk register with treatment decisions; approval and residual risk acceptance records; records from the latest assessment cycle
good_looks_like: Every assessed risk has a treatment option, planned controls, an owner, timing and an approved residual risk level. Approval is dated and recorded.
test: Obtain the register and treatment plan. Sample five risks and check each has a treatment, controls, approval and residual risk acceptance. Pass if all sampled risks are complete and approved.
baseline_risk: Risks go untreated or unaccepted, and the organization carries exposure no one has agreed to.

statement: A documented statement of applicable controls is kept. It states which controls apply, why each is included or left out, and whether each is implemented. The control list is checked against a reference control set to confirm none is missed, and the statement is updated after each treatment plan change.
why_asked: Without this statement, necessary controls can be dropped without anyone deciding to, and exclusions have no reason on record.
how_to_ask: Ask for the statement and check every control has a decision and reason. Ask how it was compared to a reference set. Example probe: "Pick a control you excluded and tell me why, and where that reason is written."
question: Does your organization keep a documented statement of which controls apply?
expected_evidence: Statement of applicable controls; comparison record against a reference control set; approval record; version history for the last two cycles
good_looks_like: The statement lists each control with applicable or not, a reason, and implementation status. A recorded comparison against a reference set shows nothing was missed. Management approves it.
test: Obtain the statement and the comparison record. Sample five controls, including two exclusions. Pass if each has a decision, a reason and an implementation status, the comparison is recorded, and the statement is approved and current.
baseline_risk: Needed controls are missed or excluded without reason, leaving unplanned gaps.

statement: Risk assessments are performed at planned intervals and when significant change is proposed or occurs. Assessments follow the defined method and results are kept. Proof is dated assessment reports covering the scope.
why_asked: Stale assessments hide new risks introduced by changes, so decisions rest on old information.
how_to_ask: Ask when assessments last ran and what triggers an extra one. Check results against the planned schedule. Example probe: "What was the last significant change, and was a risk assessment done for it?"
question: Does your organization perform risk assessments at planned intervals?
expected_evidence: Risk assessment schedule; completed assessment reports and registers; records of change-triggered assessments; records from the last two cycles
good_looks_like: Assessments follow a schedule and run on trigger events. Reports are dated, use the defined method, cover the full scope and are retained.
test: Obtain the schedule and reports. Check the last two planned assessments occurred on time and sample two significant changes for a triggered assessment. Pass if all expected assessments are on record.
baseline_risk: New or changed risks go unseen, and treatment decisions rest on out-of-date views.

statement: The risk treatment plan is carried out and the results are kept. Each treatment action has an owner and due date. Progress is tracked and completion is evidenced.
why_asked: A plan that is not carried out leaves risks as high as before while records suggest otherwise.
how_to_ask: Ask for progress on the treatment plan and pick completed items to see proof. Example probe: "Show me the evidence that your last completed treatment action reduced the risk."
question: Does your organization carry out its risk treatment plan?
expected_evidence: Treatment plan with status; completion evidence for treatment actions; overdue action report; records from the current review period
good_looks_like: Each treatment action has an owner, due date and status. Completed actions have evidence, and overdue actions are escalated and re-planned with approval.
test: Obtain the treatment plan status. Sample five actions, including completed and overdue ones. Pass if completed actions have evidence and overdue actions have a recorded escalation or revised date.
baseline_risk: Treatment is planned but not done, and risks stay at their original level.

statement: A register of legal, regulatory and contractual requirements that bear on information security is kept. The register records how each is met, with an owner or control reference. It is reviewed at least every 12 months and after relevant legal change.
why_asked: Missing requirements lead to unplanned breaches of law or contract and penalties.
how_to_ask: Ask for the register and check it covers data protection, sector rules and customer contracts. Check ownership and the last review. Example probe: "Which new law or contract term did you add last year, and who owns meeting it?"
question: Does your organization keep a current register of the legal, regulatory, or contractual requirements that bear on its information security?
expected_evidence: Legal and contractual requirements register with owners or control references; review history for the last 12 months; record of updates after legal changes
good_looks_like: The register lists each requirement with its source, owner and how it is met. It has been reviewed within the cycle and updated after relevant changes.
test: Obtain the register. Sample five requirements and check each has an owner or control reference and how it is met. Pass if the sample is complete and the register was reviewed within the last 12 months or after a relevant legal change.
baseline_risk: The organization breaches laws or contracts without knowing, facing fines and lost business.
key_settings: base: register review at least every 12 months and after relevant legal change

statement: Rules for protecting intellectual property are set, including obtaining software only from legitimate sources and staying within license terms. Software licenses are reconciled against installed or subscribed software on a defined cycle, and differences are acted on. Proof is the procedure and reconciliation record.
why_asked: Unlicensed or misused software and content brings legal claims, penalties and loss of vendor trust.
how_to_ask: Ask who manages licenses and how installed software is compared to entitlements. Example probe: "Show me the last license reconciliation and what you did about any shortfall."
question: Does your organization protect intellectual property rights, including license compliance?
expected_evidence: Intellectual property and software license procedure; software license register; reconciliation report against installed or subscribed software; records for the last review cycle
good_looks_like: A procedure covers legitimate sources and license compliance. A register of entitlements is reconciled against actual use on a set cycle, and shortfalls are fixed.
test: Obtain the procedure and the latest reconciliation. Sample five software products and compare entitlements with installed or subscribed counts. Pass if the procedure exists and the sampled products are within entitlement or have a recorded fix.
baseline_risk: Use of unlicensed software leads to legal claims, audit penalties and exposure to tampered software.

statement: The privacy laws and contractual terms that apply to the organization's processing of personal data are identified. Responsibility for privacy and personal data protection is assigned and recorded, and a current record of that processing is kept for the program scope. The record is reviewed on a defined cycle and when processing changes.
why_asked: Without knowing what personal data is processed and what rules apply, the organization cannot protect it or prove compliance.
how_to_ask: Ask who is accountable for privacy and where the record of processing sits. Check it is current. Example probe: "Show me your record of processing and the law or contract behind one entry."
question: Does your organization keep a record of its processing of personal data?
expected_evidence: Privacy policy listing applicable laws and contractual terms; record of the assignment of privacy responsibility; record of personal data processing or data inventory; review history for the last two cycles
good_looks_like: A policy names applicable privacy laws and contract terms. Responsibility for privacy is assigned and recorded. A current processing record covers the scope with purposes, data types and owners, and is updated after change.
test: Obtain the policy, role record and processing record. Sample five processing activities and check each is recorded with a purpose and owner. Pass if the laws are identified, responsibility for privacy is assigned, and the sampled records are current.
baseline_risk: Personal data is handled without clear rules or owner, leading to privacy breaches and penalties.
applicability: Applies if the organization processes personal data.

statement: Independent review of security is planned, including when it happens and what triggers an unscheduled review. An internal audit program takes account of how important the processes are and the results of earlier audits. Audits have defined criteria, scope and impartial auditors. Reviews are performed within the planned interval and results are reported to management, with evidence kept.
why_asked: Without independent review, the organization marks its own homework and misses problems its owners cannot see.
how_to_ask: Ask for the audit program and the last reports. Check auditors are independent of the area audited and results reach management. Example probe: "Who audited your last security review, and who did they report to?"
question: Does your organization have its security program independently reviewed on a planned cycle?
expected_evidence: Audit program or plan with triggers; audit scope and criteria; audit reports; auditor independence record; evidence of reporting to management; records from the last two cycles
good_looks_like: An audit plan sets frequency, methods, criteria, scope and triggers. Auditors are objective and impartial. Reports go to management, and findings flow into corrective action.
test: Obtain the audit program and last two reports. Check each audit ran within its planned interval, used impartial auditors and was reported to management. Pass if all hold and findings are logged.
baseline_risk: Weaknesses go unnoticed because the program is only checked by those who run it.

statement: The day-to-day work of each team where security controls apply is checked on a defined cycle against the documented security policies and standards. The checks test what is actually done in the work, not only what is written. Each gap between practice and policy is recorded with an action, and actions are tracked to closure. Proof is the check schedule, the check reports and the action tracker.
why_asked: Policy drift goes unseen when nobody compares practice with the written rule, and behavior slides away from what is documented.
how_to_ask: Ask which teams carry security controls and how the organization knows they work as the policy says (for example internal audit, a control self-assessment, or technical scans). Look at one recent check and what it found. Example probe: "Show me the last time someone checked what one team really does against the policy, and the actions that came out of it."
question: Does your organization regularly check that day-to-day work in teams where security controls apply follows its documented security policies?
expected_evidence: List of teams where controls apply; check schedule; check reports (audit reports, self-assessments or technical scan results); gap register with actions; records from the current review period
good_looks_like: Every team where controls apply is on a schedule. Checks compare real practice (records, settings, observation) with policy, not only documents. Each gap has an owner and a due date and is tracked to closure.
test: Obtain the list of teams where security controls apply, the check schedule and the latest check reports. Sample three teams. For each, confirm a check took place in the cycle, that it compared actual practice (records, settings or observation) with the documented policy, and that every gap has an action. Pass if every listed team is on the schedule, each sampled team was checked in the cycle on real practice, and every gap is tracked to closure or has an approved exception. Fail if a check was only a self-declaration with no supporting records.
baseline_risk: Deviations from policy persist unnoticed, and weak spots only appear in incidents or audits.
